meta.theme: urban anonymity redescribed as one side of a single arrangement rather than as a service the city has failed to supply, with the freedom to release or withhold a past set against the cost borne by whoever cannot manage alone, and the remedy narrowed to forms of recognition a person can enter and also leave

meta.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-05
meta.reviewer_notes: A scene, then the received complaint given in full strength, then the same arrangement from the other side, then the cost named without softening. The two women are the passage's structural device: they are one arrangement described twice, and the temptation is to read them as cause and effect, which is what the relationship question is built on.
meta.tone: observant, fair to the complaint, unromantic at the close

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option making the younger woman's freedom purchased out of the older one's isolation, which reads a single arrangement as a transaction between two parties; the passage says she is receiving the identical arrangement from the other end of it, which is a description of one fact twice, not of a cause and its effect. Q2's unsupported statement is the claim about attachment to families, which the passage never touches: leaving a reputation behind is not leaving people, and the woman's mother and brother are the reason the town's exchanges are described as exchanges of information. Q3's rival is the impatient reading, which cannot survive the sentence granting that the numbers are not invented and the loss not imaginary. Q4's rival is the option about defending the city against exaggeration, which is half right, since the author defends the city and expressly refuses to say the complaint has overstated anything. Q5's rival is the option about restoring a village's mutual knowledge, which the final paragraph forbids twice, once by the identity of the two facts and once by the caretaker who is not trying to be a village. Q6's rival is solitude, which the third paragraph names and then refuses in the same sentence.

paragraphs.text: She had been in the city four days when she noticed it, in a bread shop. The woman behind the counter took her money, gave her change, said something about the weather that would have been said to anybody, and turned to the next customer. Nothing had happened. That was what she noticed. In the town she had left, buying bread was also a small exchange of information: how her mother was keeping, whether the roof had been seen to, what was being said about her brother. Here she was a person buying bread, and the transaction was complete.

The complaint about this is old and it is not foolish. A man dies in a flat and is found a fortnight later. Corridors run the length of a building and the doors along them stay shut. Surveys report the proportion of residents who cannot name anybody on their own floor, and the proportion rises. Nobody who has read such an account can pretend that the numbers are invented or that the loss they describe is imaginary. Something that used to be supplied without anyone asking for it is now not supplied at all, and the people it is missing from did not choose to do without it.

Now take the same arrangement from inside the bread shop. In the town she had never introduced herself to anybody, because she had never needed to. She was her father's daughter. She was the girl who had failed an examination that the whole street knew she was sitting. She was a member of a congregation she had stopped believing in four years earlier and still attended, because leaving would have been an announcement. Every one of these went ahead of her into every room she entered, and none of it was hers to release or to withhold. What she has acquired in the city is not solitude. It is the power to decide what is known.

Two things follow from that power and they are worth separating. The first is that she can be more than one thing. She can be serious in one room and frivolous in another and studious in a third, and nobody is assembling the pieces into a single verdict, because the people in those rooms will never meet. The second is that a reputation can be ended. A small place remembers a failure for thirty years, not out of malice but out of arithmetic: there are not enough people available to talk about anything else. It is no accident that those who have most needed cities are so often the ones for whom the older arrangement had no comfortable place.

What this costs, and who pays it, should be said plainly. The same not being known that protects her is the reason nobody comes when she does not appear. Anonymity is a resource, and like other resources it is held unequally: it is worth most to a person who can manage alone and costs most to a person who cannot. The old woman in the flat above is not enjoying a freedom. She is receiving the identical arrangement from the other end of it, and calling her situation the price of somebody else's liberty does nothing whatever for her.

So the complaint is not mistaken about the facts. It is mistaken about the description. It treats not being known as something the city has failed to supply, when it is the same fact as something the city does supply, seen from the other side, and a city cannot raise the one without lowering the other, which is why exhortations to know your neighbours have never yet worked anywhere. What can be built is narrower and less romantic: forms of recognition a person is able to enter and also to leave. A caretaker who knows which flats have nobody in them is not a village and is not trying to be one. Whether that is enough is a fair question. Whether a city might simply decide to be a village is not.

questions.target_mistake: reading two descriptions of one arrangement as a transaction in which one woman's freedom is bought with the other's isolation
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the two women are the same fact described from two positions, one gaining by it and one losing by it.
questions.stem: The relation between the woman in the bread shop and the old woman in the flat above is best described as

options.A: a contrast between a generation that valued its neighbours and a later one that no longer does
options.B: a cause and its effect, the younger woman's freedom being purchased out of the older one's isolation
options.C: an illustration of the complaint stated in the second paragraph, followed by an illustration of the author's answer to it
options.D: one arrangement described from two positions, a freedom where one stands and an abandonment where the other does

explanation.expert_notice: The fifth paragraph states the relation in a single sentence and chooses its words carefully. The old woman is receiving the identical arrangement from the other end of it. Identical, and received rather than caused, which rules out both a difference of kind and a transfer between the two.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps that identity. The same not being known is said to protect one woman and to be the reason nobody comes for the other, so there is one fact with two faces rather than two facts in any sequence. The sixth paragraph generalises it, calling the thing the city fails to supply the same fact as the thing it does supply, seen from the other side.
explanation.question_type_note: A relationship question asks how two things in the passage stand to each other. Where an author uses the words identical or the same fact, the answer is an identity and not a sequence.
explanation.reading_habit: When two cases are set against each other, check whether the author says one produces the other or that both are the same thing seen differently. Causal options are the commonest way of getting that distinction wrong.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is said about generations or about what anybody values. The old woman is distinguished by not being able to manage alone, which the fifth paragraph makes a matter of circumstance rather than of attitude.
distractors.seductive_element: Stories about neighbours are usually stories about decline, and the surveys in the second paragraph supply the rising proportion that such a story needs.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage refuses this in the sentence immediately after. Calling her situation the price of somebody else's liberty is named as a description that does nothing whatever for her, and the arrangement is called identical rather than transferred.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the passage does speak of cost and of who pays, and the language of payment invites a reader to supply a payer and a beneficiary.

distractors.why_wrong: The order is the other way round and the roles are wrong. The woman in the shop opens the passage and belongs to the author's reply, while the old woman appears in the paragraph that names the cost, after the reply has been made.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage really does state a complaint and then answer it, so a reader who has the shape right and the sequence wrong will fit the two women into the frame.

questions.target_mistake: accepting a general belief about people who move away as though the passage had made a claim about their attachments
questions.stem: All of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.A: People who move to cities are on the whole less attached to their families than those who stay
options.B: A person's past can be common knowledge in a small place without their having told anybody
options.C: The worth of not being known is not the same for every person who happens to have it
options.D: A city cannot make its residents more known to one another without at the same time making them less unknown

explanation.expert_notice: Three of the four have sentences behind them. The third paragraph says she never introduced herself because she never needed to; the fifth says the resource is held unequally; the sixth says a city cannot raise the one without lowering the other. Nothing anywhere concerns how much anyone cares for their family.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The statement that cannot be inferred is the one about attachment. The passage's only family material runs the other way: the town's bread shop exchanges are about how her mother is keeping and what is being said about her brother, which are the questions of a person still connected to them. Leaving a reputation behind is not the same as leaving people, and the passage never converts one into the other.
explanation.question_type_note: In a cannot-be-inferred question three options can be anchored and one cannot. The unanchored one is usually a belief the reader already holds about the topic rather than a distortion of the text.
explanation.reading_habit: Point at a sentence for each option before choosing. If you find yourself explaining why an option is probably true of the world, you have found the exception.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph states this twice over. She had never introduced herself because she had never needed to, and each fact about her went ahead of her into every room she entered without being hers to release.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage puts it as a story about one woman, so a reader looking for a general statement of the point does not find the sentence and doubts the inference.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph says exactly this in the language of resources: anonymity is held unequally, worth most to a person who can manage alone and costing most to a person who cannot.
distractors.seductive_element: The option is pitched one level above the passage's own wording, which makes a faithful restatement look like an addition of the reader's own.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the sixth paragraph's central claim, that the two are one fact seen from two sides and that a city cannot raise the one without lowering the other. It is the reason the passage gives for the failure of every exhortation.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads as an abstract statement about cities rather than as a sentence of this passage, and readers discount options that sound like general theory.

questions.target_mistake: reading a disagreement about how to describe a fact as a denial that the fact is serious
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: he accepts every fact the complaint offers and rejects only the account of what those facts show.
questions.stem: The author's attitude towards the familiar complaint about city life is best described as

options.A: impatient with a grievance he regards as sentimental and poorly supported by its evidence
options.B: accepting of the facts it reports and unwilling to accept the description it builds on them
options.C: delighted by a freedom he believes the critics of city life have never once understood
options.D: resigned to a loss he thinks no arrangement of any kind could now do anything to reduce

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph is written for the complaint and says so: it is old and it is not foolish, the numbers are not invented, the loss is not imaginary, and nobody chose it. The sixth paragraph then separates facts from description in one sentence, saying the complaint is not mistaken about the facts and is mistaken about the description.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that separation. The author grants the evidence in the strongest terms available to him and then refuses the account built on it, and the fifth paragraph shows how far the granting goes, since he refuses even to let his own argument be used to explain the old woman's position away. An attitude option that softens the facts or dismisses the complainants has to explain those two paragraphs.
explanation.question_type_note: Attitude questions in a passage that answers a complaint are settled by how the complaint is treated, not by how warmly the author writes about his own view.
explanation.reading_habit: Find the paragraph where an author states the other side. If he strengthens it rather than weakening it, every dismissive attitude option is gone before you read the rest.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the opposite about the evidence. The complaint is called old and not foolish, and the reader is told that nobody can pretend the numbers are invented or the loss imaginary. What is refused is the description, not the support.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the author does say the complaint is mistaken, and a reader who registers the verdict without the qualification will extend it to everything the complaint contains.

distractors.why_wrong: The valence is roughly right and the volume is wrong, and the passage spends a whole paragraph on what the freedom costs and on who pays. Nothing in it delights, and the closing sentences call the buildable remedy narrower and less romantic.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph on being more than one thing is the passage's most attractive, and a reader who takes it as the conclusion will read the tone off it.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph names something that can be built, forms of recognition a person can enter and leave, and asks only whether it is enough. Denying that a city can become a village is not resignation about every possible arrangement.
distractors.seductive_element: The refusal of exhortation and the flat sentence about what does nothing whatever for the old woman both read as defeat if the last three sentences are skimmed.

questions.target_mistake: characterising the passage as a defence of city life against exaggeration, when the author concedes the evidence and disputes only its interpretation
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to name the move in a verb and an object: it redescribes a loss as one side of an arrangement, and then says who bears the other side.
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterises the passage as a whole?

options.A: an account of how much lonelier city dwellers have become than the opening scene suggests
options.B: a defence of the freedoms of city life against critics who have exaggerated its dangers beyond all recognition
options.C: a history of the idea that being unknown to one's neighbours is an affliction peculiar to life in a modern city
options.D: a redescription of a familiar loss as one side of one arrangement, with the cost of the other side named

explanation.expert_notice: The passage has three movements and the last two are the argument. A complaint is stated at full strength, the same arrangement is then viewed from the other side, and a paragraph is spent on what that costs and who pays. The sixth paragraph names the move itself: not mistaken about the facts, mistaken about the description.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps the redescription and the cost together, which is what the passage refuses to separate. Dropping the cost turns the piece into a celebration that the fifth paragraph forbids; dropping the redescription leaves nothing for the third and sixth paragraphs to do. A characterisation has to survive the sentence saying the old woman is receiving the identical arrangement.
explanation.question_type_note: A best-characterisation question wants the passage's move in a verb and an object, and both must survive the final paragraph. Where an author concedes the evidence, the move is about description rather than about facts.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what the author would have had to leave out for each candidate to be right. The correct characterisation is the one that leaves nothing on the floor.

distractors.why_wrong: That is the second paragraph, which the passage presents as somebody else's case and then answers. Offered as the whole, it makes the four paragraphs after it unaccountable.
distractors.seductive_element: The dead man and the shut doors are the passage's most striking images, and the survey figures are the only hard evidence in it.

distractors.why_wrong: The first half is close and the second contradicts the text. The author never says the dangers have been exaggerated; he says the numbers are not invented and the loss is not imaginary, and he adds a cost the complaint had not named.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the passage genuinely does defend city life, and a reader who has that much right will accept the usual reason for such a defence.

distractors.why_wrong: No history is given and no claim is made about when the condition began. The passage moves between a town and a city as two present arrangements, and its only temporal remark is that a small place remembers a failure for thirty years.
distractors.seductive_element: The opening comparison between a town and a city reads like a before and an after, which invites a reader to supply a chronology the passage never offers.

questions.target_mistake: supposing that the author's remedy is a smaller version of the village, when he defines it by the very thing a village does not allow
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that an acceptable remedy will be one a person can both enter and get out of, since the passage's objection to the old arrangement was that nothing could be withheld.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that an arrangement the author would count as a genuine remedy is one that

options.A: restores to a city street the mutual knowledge that a small town used to have
options.B: makes the cost of not being known fall on those who are best able to bear it
options.C: produces a kind of being known that a person is able to enter and also to leave
options.D: would have to reach every resident in the city equally, whatever their own circumstances were

explanation.expert_notice: The last paragraph states the test and then gives an instance of it. What can be built is recognition a person is able to enter and also to leave, and the caretaker who knows which flats are empty is offered as a case that is not a village and is not trying to be one.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that test stated as a rule. The third paragraph explains why the condition matters: what the town took from her was not company but the power to release or withhold, since everything about her went ahead of her into every room. A remedy that restored knowledge without restoring that power would reproduce exactly what she left, which is why the author defines his remedy by the exit rather than by the amount of knowing.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question about a remedy is answered by the defect the author diagnosed, not by the loss he described. Look for the condition that his diagnosis makes necessary.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author proposes something narrower than the obvious cure, ask what the obvious cure would bring back. The answer is usually the thing his first argument was against.

distractors.why_wrong: The sixth paragraph rules this out twice, once by saying a city cannot raise the one without lowering the other and once by denying that the caretaker is a village or is trying to be one. Its closing sentence calls the question of a city deciding to be a village not a fair one.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is the remedy the complaint implies, and the second paragraph has been written to make the reader want it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage records that the cost falls unequally and refuses to treat that as settled by any description. It proposes nothing about redistributing the burden, and says that calling the old woman's position a price does nothing whatever for her.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the fair-minded conclusion the fifth paragraph is heading towards, and it uses the paragraph's own vocabulary of cost and capacity.

distractors.why_wrong: Equality of reach is never made a requirement of anything. The passage observes that the resource is unequally held and then specifies its remedy by a different property altogether, whether a person can get out of it.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph on unequal holding makes equality feel like the criterion the author must be working towards, so a reader supplies it in place of the one he states.

questions.target_mistake: reading the sentence that names solitude without the sentence that immediately refuses it
questions.stem: According to the passage, what the woman has acquired by moving to the city is

options.A: solitude, of a kind the town she left had never allowed her to have at all
options.B: authority over which facts about her the people she meets are in a position to know
options.C: the security of a place in which nothing whatever about her can be found out
options.D: a reputation she will now be able to build up again from nothing at all

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph ends with two short sentences that exist to be read together. What she has acquired is not solitude; it is the power to decide what is known. The first of the pair names the wrong answer and the second supplies the right one.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option restates the second of those sentences. The paragraph has just listed the things that used to go ahead of her into every room without being hers to release or withhold, so the gain is control over disclosure rather than absence of company, which is also why the next paragraph can describe her being seen by three different sets of people.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question often turns on a sentence the author wrote in order to reject something. Read the sentence after the one that seemed to answer the question.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage says not X but Y, expect both to appear among the options. The rejected term is placed there by the author himself, which is what makes it the strongest wrong answer.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage names solitude only to deny it, in the sentence immediately before the answer. The fourth paragraph then shows her in three different rooms full of people, which is not a description of anybody's solitude.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the word is in the passage, it is the natural meaning of moving to a city alone, and the second paragraph has filled the reader's mind with shut doors.

distractors.why_wrong: Deciding what is known is not the same as nothing being discoverable. The passage gives her a power over disclosure and never claims that the city conceals anything from anyone who looks.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the same idea at a higher strength, and strength reads as precision when a reader is matching an option to a remembered sentence.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says a reputation can be ended, which is the removal of an old verdict rather than the construction of a new one. Nothing is said about what she will build, and the point of the paragraph is that no single verdict is being assembled.
distractors.seductive_element: Ending a reputation and starting again sound like the same story, and readers complete the second half without noticing the passage stopped at the first.

vocabulary.passage_use: a member of a congregation she had stopped believing in
vocabulary.meaning_here: the body of people who worship together at one place
the condition of not being identifiable to the people around you

vocabulary.passage_use: exhortations to know your neighbours have never yet worked anywhere
not out of malice but out of arithmetic
vocabulary.meaning_here: the sheer number of people available, treated as the cause

mentor.challenge: A familiar complaint is given every fact it asks for, and then answered anyway. Work out exactly what the author disagrees with, because it is not any of the evidence.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The familiar lament about not being known in cities gets its facts granted in full and its description refused, because not being known is the same fact as being able to decide what is known, seen from the other side, so a city cannot raise one without lowering the other, and the only remedy available is the narrow one of recognition a person can enter and also leave.
mentor.main_idea: City anonymity is usually described as something the city has failed to supply. The author accepts every fact behind that description and rejects the description itself. What the newcomer gains is not solitude but control over what is known about her, which lets her be several things at once and lets an old verdict end. The cost is real and falls on whoever cannot manage alone, and since the two are one fact, no exhortation can remove the cost without removing the freedom. What can be built is recognition a person can get out of.
mentor.simple_explanation:
A woman has been in a big city four days. She buys bread, and the shopkeeper says something about the weather and turns to the next customer. Nothing happens. That is what she notices. Back home, buying bread also meant being asked about her mother, the roof, her brother.

The usual complaint about this is serious and the author says so. People die in flats and are found a fortnight later. Nobody knows anyone on their own corridor. The surveys are real and the loss is real and nobody chose it.

But turn it round and look from her side. In her town she never had to introduce herself, because everyone already knew who she was: her father's daughter, the girl who failed that examination in front of everybody, a member of a church she had privately given up on but still attended because leaving would have been news. All of that arrived in the room before she did, and none of it was hers to hand over or keep back. So what she has got in the city is not loneliness. It is the ability to choose what people know.

Two things come from that. She can be different things in different places, because the people in those places will never compare notes. And a bad reputation can actually end, which in a small town it cannot, simply because there are not enough people there to talk about anything else. That is why cities have always been full of people the old arrangement had no comfortable room for.

Now the cost, stated plainly. The same not being known that protects her is exactly why nobody notices when she does not come out. Being unknown is a resource, and it is worth a lot if you can cope on your own and it is expensive if you cannot. The old woman upstairs is not enjoying anything. She is getting the same arrangement from the other end, and telling her that her situation is the price of someone else's freedom helps her not at all.

So the complaint has the facts right and the description wrong. It thinks the city has failed to provide something. In fact the thing it has not provided and the thing it has provided are one and the same, looked at from two sides, which is why telling people to get to know their neighbours has never worked anywhere. What you can actually build is smaller: kinds of being known that you can walk into and walk out of. A caretaker who knows which flats are empty is not a village, and is not pretending to be. Whether that is enough is worth arguing about. Whether a city could simply choose to be a village is not.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage agrees with the complaint about everything except what the complaint means, and readers find that combination hard to hold, so they either soften the facts or turn the author into a critic of the complainants. The second difficulty is the pair of women. They are one arrangement described twice, and everything about the way passages usually work encourages a reader to make them a cause and an effect. The third is the ending, which refuses the obvious remedy and offers a much smaller one, so a reader who has followed the argument this far still tends to attribute to the author the cure the complaint implies.
mentor.author_intention: To stop a reader from treating being unknown as a hole in city life, by showing that it is the underside of something the same city supplies, and then to prevent that argument from being used to dismiss the people it costs most.

paragraph_journey.note: A woman buys bread in a new city and nothing happens. At home the same purchase would have come with questions about her family.
The usual objection, given its full strength: the man found a fortnight later, the shut doors, the surveys. The author says the numbers are not invented.
In the town everything about her arrived before she did and none of it was hers to withhold. What she has gained is not solitude but control over what is known.
She can be more than one thing, because the rooms never meet. And a reputation can end, which in a small place it cannot, for want of anyone else to discuss.
The same fact means nobody comes when she does not appear. It is worth most to whoever can manage alone, and the old woman upstairs is getting it from the other end.
The complaint has the facts and not the description. The two are one fact, so exhortation fails, and what can be built is recognition you can enter and leave.

mentor.tone_progression: It begins in plain narrative, almost neutral; becomes serious and concessive while the complaint is stated; warms noticeably through the two paragraphs on what the newcomer has gained; then cools and hardens as the cost is named; and ends dry and deliberately unromantic, refusing the consoling remedy and offering a smaller one.
key_transitions: 'Now take the same arrangement from inside the bread shop.' (opening of paragraph 3) — the same facts are given a second description, which is the whole of the argument.
'What she has acquired in the city is not solitude. It is the power to decide what is known.' (close of paragraph 3) — the wrong answer is named and replaced in two sentences.
'The old woman in the flat above is not enjoying a freedom.' (paragraph 5) — the author refuses to let his own argument absorb the case that tells against it.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers finish with one of two wrong models. The first has the author saying that the complaint about lonely cities is overdone, which requires ignoring a paragraph written to strengthen it and a paragraph written to price it. The second has him proposing that cities recover the village, which the last paragraph refuses twice. Both errors come from the same habit: taking a passage that answers a complaint to be a passage that disputes the complaint's evidence, when what is being disputed is the sentence the evidence is put into.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers a cause and effect where the passage states an identity, a belief about families the text never touches, impatience in place of concession, a defence against exaggeration where the evidence was granted, the village restored where the author rules it out, and solitude in place of the sentence that refuses it. Deciding whether an option belongs to the complaint, the reply, the cost or the remedy answers all six.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author grants all of an opponent's evidence, stop looking for the fact he disputes and start looking for the sentence he would rewrite. Passages of this shape turn on description rather than on data, and their questions are built out of the gap between agreeing about what happened and agreeing about what it means. The same habit protects you at the close, where such authors characteristically refuse the remedy their opponent's description implies and propose a narrower one of their own.
mentor.real_world: The same double description covers a good deal of modern life: a job that can be left, which is also a job with nobody obliged to keep you; a family arrangement with no fixed duties, which is also one with no assured help; a profession with no licence to lose, which is also one with no standing to rely on. In each case the freedom and the exposure are the same fact from two positions.
mentor.takeaway: Not being known and being able to choose what is known are the same fact, and which of the two you experience depends on whether you can manage alone.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the freedoms you value most would disappear if everyone around you compared what they knew about you?
